title: Bear Gap off the Highs
teaches: The bear gap off the highs as we teach it today: a read, not a trade. The first gap down since a top that closes down 5% or more in the lower half leaves a zone of resistance. A close above the zone's top edge fills the gap and the read is off. The fall is measured, not traded; a retest short stays under the 200-day, needs the market's help, and is never taken at the gap-day close by reflex.

walkthroughs.title: VRSN, July 2008: the full window
steps: VRSN topped June 4, 2008. A month later, July 7, it opened 3.4% lower and closed down 9.5% on 6.1x volume.
A full window: the whole day traded under the prior day's low. That leaves a zone from 35.52 up to 36.74.
July 11 the bounce runs into the zone's bottom edge and gets turned back. That's the read.
A short from there would have worked. But we picked ten winners to study. We teach the read here, not the entry.

walkthroughs.title: DLTR, January 2020: the cleanest chart
steps: DLTR, the cleanest chart of the bunch. It topped October 22, 2019, and sat just 5.1% off that high.
November 26, earnings: it opens 14.8% lower and closes down 15.2% on 15.1x volume. The first gap since the top.
A flat five-week bounce stalls at the 20 EMA, 94.25, still under the 200-day. January 2, 2020 it's turned back.
A short there worked, but the 2020 market did a lot of the work. We teach the read, not the entry.

walkthroughs.title: CIEN, September 2017: a good gap in a strong market
steps: This one failed, and the chart wasn't the problem. CIEN, August 31, 2017: opens 8.7% lower, closes down 11.0% on 11.0x volume.
A textbook gap day. 19 sessions later it's turned back at the 20-day EMA, under its own 200-day.
But the market was strong, QQQ 1.0% over its 50-day. This short needs a weak market, Red or Orange on our filter.
A short off that turn got stopped the next session. A good gap alone isn't enough.

questions.q: A stock gaps down hard off its highs and closes near the lows. How do we treat a bear gap like that?
choices: A level to read, not a trade
A short to take at the close
A dip to buy under the gap
questions.answer: A level to read, not a trade
questions.why: A level to read. We don't have a trade on this one. We mark the gap and watch how price acts under it. If you own the stock, it's a warning. If you're thinking short, never at the gap-day close. That stop sits way up over the high of a big down day, and big drops bounce. And any short we teach is only for traders who've already made $1 million trading. Read it first.
questions.lesson_line: A bear gap is a level to read. We watch it, we don't trade it.

wrong.A short to take at the close: That's the reflex short. Your stop sits way up over the high of a big down day, and big drops bounce first.
wrong.A dip to buy under the gap: Buying right under an open gap puts you under a pile of trapped sellers. Wait for a fill or a base.
wrong.A gap that'll fill soon: Don't count on it. A breakaway gap on heavy volume can sit open a long time.

questions.q: What's that zone going to act like?
questions.why: Resistance. Think about who's sitting in there. Everyone who bought before the gap is underwater. The first rally back gives them a chance to get out near even, and they take it. That's supply. So price tends to stall in the zone. It's a speed bump though, not a wall. A close back above the top edge fills the gap and the read is done. LDOS rallied right into it here, so you watch for sellers.
questions.lesson_line: An open gap down leaves sellers overhead. Expect the rally to stall there.

wrong.Support for a long: The zone sits above price, not under it. Overhead it's supply, not support.
wrong.A magnet that fills fast: Don't plan on a fill. Gaps like this can sit open a long time, and rallies stall in the zone first.
wrong.Nothing, just empty space: Empty on the chart, but full of trapped buyers. That's why price stalls there.

questions.simple: Resistance, because buyers trapped above the gap use the rally to get out near even.

deeper.counter: Bulkowski calls gaps places of weak support or resistance. Treat the zone as a place a rally may stall, not a promise. Schaeffer's makes the same point: some stocks just can't get through a bear gap's zone.

reasons: proposed card criterion (bg.level_resistance), though three outside publishers agree

questions.story: This stock gapped down off its highs and left an open gap overhead. Now it has rallied back up into that gap zone.

questions.q: Two stocks gap down off their highs. One closes near its lows, the other near its highs. The weak close is the stronger bear gap.
questions.why: True. The close tells you who won the day. Down near the low of the day, sellers pressed right into the bell and nobody stepped in. The bad news worked. Back up near the high, buyers took a big piece of the gap back. That's a different chart. If it closes all the way back above yesterday's close, it's a News Failure, and that's a buy for us, not a short. Check the close before you mark anything.
questions.lesson_line: Check the close. Down near the lows, the bad news worked.
questions.simple: True, because a close near the lows means sellers won the day and buyers never showed up.

reasons: proposed card criterion (bg.gap_day) awaiting the owner; Fleckenstein agrees on the close

deeper.counter: Fleckenstein, who wrote up this gap-down short, asked for a close in the lower half of the day's range. Read it by eye, not as a hard line: weak close, sellers won.

questions.q: Which of these gap days leaves a full window on the chart?
choices: Its high stays under yesterday's low
questions.answer: Its high stays under yesterday's low
questions.why: The one whose high stays under yesterday's low. Then the two bars never touch, and you see daylight between them. That empty space is the window, and it's the zone we mark. A lower open alone isn't enough. If price trades back up into yesterday's range, there's no window left. All ten examples we studied for this lesson were full windows.
questions.lesson_line: No overlap with yesterday's bar. That's a window.

wrong.It opens under yesterday's close: That's just a lower open. The day can rally back into yesterday's range and leave no window.
wrong.It closes under yesterday's close: That's a red day. Nothing about it leaves empty space on the chart.
wrong.It opens under yesterday's high: That open can sit right inside yesterday's range. No gap at all.

questions.simple: The gap day's high stays under yesterday's low, so the two bars never touch on the chart.

reasons: full window is a proposed card term; the definition itself is ChartSchool's

questions.q: Which gap do we read first off a top?
choices: The first gap down since the top
The third gap off the same top
Any gap down in a long decline
A gap down inside a base
questions.answer: The first gap down since the top
questions.why: The first gap down since the top. Later gaps off the same top did worse.
questions.lesson_line: Read the first crack off the top, not the third.

wrong.The third gap off the same top: Later gaps off the same top did worse.
wrong.Any gap down in a long decline: Off the highs means off a top, not a decline already well under way.
wrong.A gap down inside a base: A base has no top to gap away from. The read starts from a top.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The gap day closes down at least ___ and in the lower half of its range.
questions.why: 5%. Our card's gap day closes down at least 5% from the prior close, and in the lower half of its range. Both tests must pass. Fleckenstein also wanted the close in the lower half of the day's range. The 5% line is our card's proposed line, so it may still change.
questions.lesson_line: Down at least 5%, in the lower half.
questions.simple: The gap day must close down at least 5% and in the lower half of its range.

reasons: the 5% rests on one card line (c03)
a proposed number that may change

questions.q: What's that gap telling you, and what do you do?
choices: A warning, let your stop decide
Sell it all at the open
questions.answer: A warning, let your stop decide
questions.why: It's a warning, and your stop makes the call. You planned this HWM trade with a stop, so let it do its job. If the open is still above your stop, you hold and keep trailing. If the gap opened through it, our gap rule kicks in. The low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. What you don't do is buy more or push the stop lower. We buy full size at one price with one stop, and the stop only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: A bear gap on a stock you own is a warning. Your stop does the rest.

wrong.A dip, buy more shares: That's adding to a loser, and we never do it. Your full size went in at one price, with one stop.
wrong.A risk, widen your stop: The stop only moves up. Giving it room is how a small loss turns into a big one.
wrong.Sell it all at the open: That's panic, not a plan. If the stop isn't hit, the stop decides. If it gapped through, the first 30 minutes do.

questions.simple: It's a warning, so let the stop you already have make the call. Don't add and don't widen it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, A5, B20)

questions.story: You own this stock. It has been working near its highs. This morning it gaps down hard off those highs.

questions.q: The bounce on this chart just reached the open gap zone overhead. That's a good spot to start a new long.
questions.why: False. You'd be buying right into the sellers. Everyone trapped above the gap wants out near even, and the first rally into the zone is where they sell. This is MDT, and I'd rather let it prove itself. Wait for a close back above the zone's top edge, a fill, or for a base to build under it. Then you've got an area to risk against.
questions.lesson_line: Don't buy right under an open bear gap. Let it fill or base first.
questions.simple: False, because the open gap above is where trapped buyers sell, so wait for a fill or a base.

reasons: one source: the criteria card
proposed card criterion (bg.long_warning) awaiting the owner

questions.q: A bear gap gets filled within a few days, with a close back above the zone. What's that telling you?
choices: It was only a partial gap
questions.why: Buyers are strong. They took back the whole gap in a few days, and a broken stock doesn't do that. Once it closes above the zone's top edge, the read is off. No level, no short. If anything, that stock just showed you strength. Keep it on your radar for that reason instead.
questions.lesson_line: A quick fill is strength. The read is over.

wrong.Sellers are strong here: Sellers had the gap and lost it. A fill is buyers winning.
wrong.It was only a partial gap: Partial or full is about where it opened. It says nothing about how fast it fills.
wrong.The zone is resistance now: After a close over the top edge there's no zone left to resist anything.

questions.simple: A quick fill means buyers took back the whole gap, so the read is off and the stock is showing strength.

reasons: the key rests on one card line (c06)
the zone's top edge waits on a held decision (D-100)

questions.q: A stock opens under yesterday's close but stays above yesterday's low. That leaves a full window.
questions.why: False. You've got a partial gap. The open dipped under yesterday's close, but price is still trading inside yesterday's range. For a window you need the whole day, the high included, under yesterday's low. Then there's real empty space on the chart, and that space is the zone you mark.
questions.lesson_line: Inside yesterday's range is a partial gap. All day under yesterday's low is a window.
questions.simple: False, because the stock is still inside yesterday's range, and a window needs the whole day under yesterday's low.

deeper.trap: ChartSchool's gap-trading page calls any open under yesterday's low a full gap down. A window asks more: the day's high has to stay under yesterday's low too. A stock can open under yesterday's low, rally back above it, and leave no window at all.

reasons: fixed before (a publisher counted twice)

questions.q: A breakaway gap down is the kind that starts a new leg lower. What comes right before one?
choices: A run up, a top or a range
The tail end of a long decline
The middle of a fast drop
questions.answer: A run up, a top or a range
questions.why: A run up, a top or a sideways range. ChartSchool says a bearish breakaway gap forms after an extended advance, an extended top or a consolidation. That's why we care about the first gap off the highs. It's the stock breaking away from where it's been living. A gap at the end of a long fall is different. That's an exhaustion gap, and it shows up near the end of the move, not the start.
questions.lesson_line: Breakaway gaps down come off tops and ranges. Late in a fall, it's exhaustion.

wrong.The tail end of a long decline: That's an exhaustion gap. It shows up near the end of a move, not the start.
wrong.One quiet day: One day isn't a top or a range. There's nothing to break away from.
wrong.The middle of a fast drop: A gap mid-drop isn't breaking away from anything. The breakaway leaves the top or the range.

questions.simple: It comes after a long run up, a top or a sideways range, when the stock breaks away from where it lived.

reasons: the key rests mainly on one ChartSchool sentence (g02); Kell's page could not be re-read on 2026-11-12

deeper.example: Kell points to DECK: a gap down from highs, followed by a Wedge Drop, marked its 2021 top.

questions.q: Two stocks gap down at the open, one by a little and one by a lot. Which one is more likely to keep dropping?
questions.why: The big gap. QuantRocket tested it and found stocks tend to recover after small down gaps and keep dropping after large ones. Makes sense. A small gap is noise, the kind that gets bought by lunch. A big one means something changed, and holders are still getting out. Keep in mind it was one vendor's same-day test, bought just after the open and held to the close. A lean, not a promise.
questions.lesson_line: Small gaps get bought. Big ones tend to keep going.

wrong.The small gap: Other way around. Small down gaps tend to recover.
wrong.Both drop about the same: The test found they don't. Size changed what happened next.
wrong.Both tend to recover: Only the small ones did. The big ones kept dropping.

questions.simple: The big gap, because big gaps tend to keep falling while small ones tend to get bought back.

reasons: the key rests on one vendor backtest (m02), named in the stem
f03 does not speak to recovery, so it is not a second agreeing publisher

questions.q: Prior close 50.00. The gap day closes at 47.00. The close is down what percent?
questions.why: 6.0%. Divide the drop by the prior close: (50.00 - 47.00) / 50.00 is 6.0%. That clears our card's 5% line. Measure from the prior close, not from the gap day's open. The close must also sit in the lower half of the day's range, a separate test.
questions.lesson_line: Do the division. Down 6.0% clears the 5% bar.
questions.simple: The close is down 6.0%, because you divide the drop by the prior close of 50.00.

reasons: computed key

wrong.6.4%: Divided by the close, not the prior close.
wrong.3.0%: Used the dollar drop as a percent.
wrong.94.0%: Gave the close as a share of the prior close.

questions.q: The gap day's high is 44.00. Yesterday's low was 46.00. How wide is the zone a bounce has to get through to fill the gap?
questions.why: $2.00. The window is the empty space between the two bars, 46.00 minus 44.00. That's the zone a bounce has to chew through. Price can poke into it and still fail. Only a close back above 46.00, the top edge, fills it. Mark both edges the night before so you're not doing math mid-session.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the window from the gap day's high up to yesterday's low.
questions.simple: The window is 2.00 wide, from the gap day's high of 44.00 up to yesterday's low of 46.00.

reasons: computed key
fixed before (LDOS's prior close was read as its low)

wrong.$1.00: That's only halfway up the window.

questions.q: A bounce runs up to the gap zone. What does the day that rejects it look like?
choices: Tags it, closes weak under it
questions.answer: Tags it, closes weak under it
questions.why: It tags the level and closes weak back under it. Both parts matter. The tag shows price got to where the sellers are. The weak close, down near the low of the day, shows they won. A day that touches the level but finishes up near its high means buyers won it. No rejection there. And a close above the zone's top edge fills the gap, which ends the read.
questions.lesson_line: Tag the level, close weak under it. That's a rejection.

wrong.Gaps through it and holds: Holding above the level is the opposite. Buyers won that one.
wrong.Closes above it on volume: That's a break. Above the zone's top edge it fills the gap.
wrong.Any red candle near it: Near isn't enough. It has to tag the level and close weak back under it.

questions.simple: It touches the level, then closes back under it near the lows, so you can see the sellers won.

reasons: rests on one card line (c17)

questions.q: A bear gap leaves a full window. How do you draw the zone on your chart?
choices: A band, gap high to prior low
A line at the gap day's high
A line at the prior day's low
A band over the gap day's range
questions.answer: A band, gap high to prior low
questions.why: As a band. The bottom edge is the gap day's high, the top edge is the prior day's low. On an overnight gap with no full window, the top goes up to the prior close. Draw both edges because they do different jobs. Price poking above the bottom edge is just a test. Only a close above the top edge fills the gap and ends the read. One line hides that, and you'll call it filled too early.
questions.lesson_line: The zone is a band, not a line. Only a close over the top edge fills it.

wrong.A line at the gap day's high: That's just the bottom edge. A poke above it isn't a fill.
wrong.A line at the prior day's low: That's just the top edge. You lose where the zone starts.
wrong.A band over the gap day's range: That's the gap day's own bar. The zone is the empty space above it.

questions.simple: Draw one band from the gap day's high to the prior day's low, since only a close over the top fills it.

deeper.trap: Each single line is a real edge, so it feels right. But a close above the bottom edge isn't a fill. Only a close above the top edge fills the gap, so draw the whole band.

reasons: rests on one source, the card (c32, c06)
held decision D-100 (which line is the zone)
fixed before (re-keyed onto the D-100 default)

questions.q: It's the close. Do you short it here?
choices: Yes, at half the usual size
No, short a break of today's low
questions.story: The gap day. It opens 7.6% lower and closes down 20.0% on 12.3x its average volume, in the lower half of its range.
questions.why: No. Never short the gap-day close by reflex. This is EEFT, and look at what you'd be risking against. It opened 7.6% lower and closed down 20.0%, so the high of the day sits way above your entry. That's a huge stop. It's also stretched far under its 9 EMA, and big drops like this bounce. Any short comes later, on the retest under the 200-day, as price trades through a trigger. And shorting is only for traders who've made $1 million trading.
questions.lesson_line: Don't short the gap-day close. Big drops bounce.

wrong.Yes, sellers won on volume: They did win the day. That's why it's stretched, and stretched stocks snap back.
wrong.Yes, at half the usual size: Smaller size doesn't fix a bad entry. The stop is still way up over the high.
wrong.No, short a break of today's low: Too soon. A short, if any, comes after the bounce fails, under the 200-day.

questions.simple: Wait, because shorting the close puts your stop way up over the day's high, and big drops tend to bounce first.

deeper.trap: The weak close and the heavy volume feel like proof, and that's the trap. In Bulkowski's dead-cat sample, big one-day drops bounced 28% on average.

reasons: proposed card gate (bg.no_reflex_short) awaiting the owner; Bulkowski and Fleckenstein agree

questions.q: What are you looking at?
choices: A News Failure, not a bear gap
A bear gap, it opened 6% lower
A Parabolic Short on the news
A full window off the highs
questions.story: A stock opens down 6% on bad news. Buyers step in all day, and it closes back above the prior close.
questions.answer: A News Failure, not a bear gap
questions.why: A News Failure. It opened down 6% on bad news and buyers took it all back by the close. The news failed. That's bullish, and it's a buy setup for us, not a short. A bear gap is the opposite. The bad news works and the stock closes weak, down near the lows. The open never decides it. The close does.
questions.lesson_line: Bad news, then a close above yesterday's close. The news failed. That's a buy.

wrong.A bear gap, it opened 6% lower: The open doesn't decide it. A bear gap closes weak, and this one closed up.
wrong.A Parabolic Short on the news: A Parabolic Short gaps up on its climax day after a run. This one gapped down.
wrong.A full window off the highs: It closed above yesterday's close, so the bars overlap. No window.

questions.simple: It's a News Failure, because buyers took back the whole drop and it closed above yesterday's close.

reasons: one source: the criteria card
proposed lookalike line awaiting the owner
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Is that a bear gap you'd mark?
questions.story: The gap day. It opens 6.0% lower, then buyers step in. It closes down 4.2%, up at 70% of the day's range.
questions.why: No. This was CMCSA on 2015-08-24. It opened 6.0% lower, but buyers took a good chunk of that back. Down 4.2% at the close and sitting at 70% of the day's range is a strong finish for a gap day. The sellers didn't win. That looks more like a News Failure starting than a bear gap. For a bear gap you want the bad news to work, with the close down near the lows. Read the close, not the open.
questions.lesson_line: The close is the test, not the open.

wrong.Yes, it opened 6.0% lower: The open isn't the test. By the close, buyers had taken a lot of it back.
wrong.Yes, it still closed red: Red isn't enough. It closed at 70% of its range, a strong finish.
wrong.Yes, any gap down counts: Only one the sellers win. This one closed high in its range.

questions.simple: No, because it closed well up off its lows, which shows buyers took the gap back.

reasons: one source: our own scan and card (repo only)
proposed card criterion (bg.gap_day) awaiting the owner

questions.q: You're eyeing a bear gap for a short. Where does the stock need to be against its 200-day?
questions.why: Under it. We short only stocks below the 200-day. Above it, a gap down is more often a pullback in a leader than a top, and leaders get bought. Under it, the stock has already lost its long-term trend, so you're shorting with that trend, not against it. The one exception in our rules is a parabolic short, and a bear gap isn't one.
questions.lesson_line: No shorts above the 200-day. Under it only.

wrong.Above it: Above the 200-day a gap down is more often a leader pulling back. We don't short those.
wrong.Right on it: On the line is still undecided. We want it under.
wrong.Either side is fine: Not for us. The 200-day is a hard line for shorts.

questions.simple: Under it, because we only short stocks below the 200-day, where they have already lost the long-term trend.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: A $6 stock that trades $5 million a day just left a clean bear gap. It's worth marking and watching.
questions.why: False. It doesn't make our list in the first place. We only look at stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one fails both. Cheap, thin stocks get pushed around, and getting out can be ugly. Clean chart or not, we don't even watch it.
questions.lesson_line: Under $10 or under $20 million a day, we don't even watch it.
questions.simple: False, because we only watch stocks at $10 or more that trade $20 million a day, and this one fails both.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: Fleckenstein, who wrote up the gap-down short, puts it on at the close of the gap day.
questions.why: False. He waited. In his words, the short seller should wait for the bounce to occur and exhaust itself. Then he shorts after the stock resumes its decline. We agree. Shorting the gap-day close puts your stop way up over the high and walks you right into the bounce.
questions.lesson_line: The short comes after the bounce, not at the gap-day close.
questions.simple: False, because he waited for the bounce to run out and shorted as the drop started again.

reasons: two outside publishers agree, and the card matches

deeper.counter: Bulkowski says the same in his dead-cat bounce work: short the stock at the top of the bounce and ride price lower.

questions.q: A breakaway gap down on heavy volume tends to get filled soon.
questions.why: False. Don't plan around a fill. A breakaway gap on heavy volume can sit open a long time. Heavy volume means a lot of holders changed their minds at once. Those sellers don't disappear in a week. So if you're long under one, you're waiting under supply. Let the stock show you a fill or a base first.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy-volume gaps down don't owe you a fill.
questions.simple: False, because a big gap on heavy volume can stay open a long time, so don't count on a quick fill.

deeper.counter: ChartSchool's warning is the same: don't assume a breakaway gap on good volume will be filled soon. Don't flip it into the opposite rule either. Plenty of gaps fill later.

reasons: the key rests on one ChartSchool sentence (g03)
fixed before (leaned on a different population)

questions.q: Our app's market filter reads Green, Yellow, Orange or Red. Which readings give a bear gap retest short some help?
questions.why: Red or Orange. The market reading is our app's market filter. Green is a healthy market, Red is one under real pressure. A short needs the market falling with it. In Red we're mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day. In a strong market even a clean short gets squeezed. Two textbook retests in our study got stopped right away in a strong uptrend. Treat the reading as a guide. And shorts are only for traders who've already made $1 million trading.
questions.lesson_line: A short needs the market's help. Red or Orange.

wrong.Yellow only: Yellow means smaller and fewer longs. It isn't the help a short needs.
wrong.Any reading works: The market decides a lot. A short fighting a strong market is a coin flip at best.
wrong.Green or Yellow: That's a market going up. Clean shorts got stopped right away in a strong uptrend.

questions.simple: Red or Orange, because a short needs the market falling with it, and a strong market squeezes shorts.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D46, F65)

questions.q: A bounce is heading up into an open falling window. In Bulkowski's study, how often did a gap like that hold price back?
questions.why: 25% of the time. Bulkowski counted how often a minor high formed inside a falling window before price closed the gap. One in four. So the zone is a speed bump, not a wall. That's exactly why we don't short a stock just for reaching it. We wait for the rejection day to show us the sellers really showed up.
questions.lesson_line: A gap is a speed bump, not a wall. Wait for the rejection.

wrong.5% of the time: Too low. He found a high formed inside the gap 25% of the time.
wrong.75% of the time: That's flipped. 25% held, so most didn't.
wrong.Almost every time: No gap is a wall. Most rallies in his sample didn't stall inside it.

questions.simple: Only about a quarter of the time, so treat the gap as a speed bump and wait for the rejection.

deeper.counter: A gap doesn't have to stop every rally to matter. Bulkowski calls gaps places of weak support or resistance. Read the zone as a place price may stall, and let a close above its top edge end the read.

reasons: the number rests on one publisher (Bulkowski)
a study statistic that can be revised
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Three straight up days to a new high. Day four gaps up, then sells off and closes red. Which setup is it?
questions.why: Parabolic Short. You've got a burst up, then a climax day that gaps up and closes red. A bear gap is a different animal. It gaps down, and there's no burst right before it. Look at the direction of the gap first. Up and red after a run is the climax. Down off a top is the bear gap.
questions.lesson_line: Gap up and close red after a burst is a Parabolic Short. Gap down off a top is a bear gap.

wrong.Bear gap off the highs: A bear gap gaps down. This one gapped up.
wrong.News Failure: A News Failure opens down on bad news and closes above the prior close.
wrong.Parabolic Long: That's a burst down into a climax gap down. This burst went up.

questions.simple: It's a Parabolic Short, because the top day gaps up and closes red after a run, while a bear gap gaps down.

reasons: rests on one source, the card (c23, c22)
the parabolic burst waits on held decisions (D-009, D-013)
fixed before

questions.q: Our study short in DLTR was 93.01, the stop 94.71. How far above the entry is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 1.8%. (94.71 - 93.01) / 93.01. A clean rejection candle gives a stop well inside the usual 3% line.
questions.lesson_line: Stop distance in percent: the gap between stop and entry, over the entry.

questions.q: Study short at 93.01, stop 94.71. Where is 3R, where a third is covered?
questions.why: 87.91. One R is the stop 94.71 minus the entry 93.01. Three of those under the entry is 87.91, where we cover a third.
questions.lesson_line: For a short, 3R sits under the entry. Mark it before the open.

questions.q: Our study ran 359 retest shorts and 311 were stopped out. What percent were stopped?
questions.why: 86.6%. 311 divided by 359. The level is a good read, but the short off it is a hard trade.
questions.lesson_line: Most study shorts were stopped. Respect the stop, not the story.

questions.q: In our study of 359 retest shorts, about what share reached 3R?
questions.why: About a quarter: 25.3% reached 3R and 14.2% reached 5R before the stop. It is a hard trade even when the read is right.
questions.lesson_line: Roughly one in four study shorts reached 3R.

questions.q: What's the zone now, and who's it for?
questions.story: A stock gaps up out of a base and runs. Weeks later it pulls back into that gap zone.
questions.why: Support, for a long. A gap up leaves a zone under price. Buyers who missed the move tend to defend it when price comes back. That's our Gap Support setup. The bear gap is the mirror image. Gap down, zone overhead, and sellers defend it. Same mechanics, opposite side of price. So before you call the zone anything, check which way the gap went.
questions.lesson_line: Same mechanics, opposite line. A gap up leaves support.

wrong.Resistance, for a short: That's the bear gap, a gap down. This one gapped up.
wrong.Resistance, for a long: The zone sits under price. It's support, not a ceiling.
wrong.Nothing, the gap is gone: Price back in the zone is the test, not the end. That's where Gap Support gets bought.

questions.simple: Support for a long, because a gap up leaves a zone under price that buyers defend on the pullback.

reasons: proposed lookalike line on the card; ChartSchool agrees

deeper.counter: ChartSchool says a downside breakout point becomes resistance. Gap Support is the same idea flipped: the zone a gap up leaves under price.

questions.q: Is this a short for us?
choices: Yes, the gap was big enough
Yes, big gaps tend to keep going
questions.story: A leader gapped down off its highs and the bounce got turned back. The rejection day closed 5.9% above its 200-day. A friend says short it.
questions.why: No. TSLA closed 5.9% above its 200-day, and we don't short above it. A gap down in a stock still over its 200-day is more often a pullback in a leader. Leaders get bought on pullbacks. Shorting one means standing in front of the buyers we'd normally be joining. Your friend is reading the gap. Read the 200-day first.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day, a gap down in a leader is a pullback, not a short.

wrong.Yes, the gap was big enough: Gap size doesn't move the 200-day. It's still above it.
wrong.Yes, big gaps tend to keep going: Sometimes they do. We still don't short above the 200-day.
wrong.No, we never short anything: We do short, below the 200-day. This one's above it.

questions.simple: No, because it's still above its 200-day, and a gap in a leader up there is a pullback, not a top.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: Where does that leave the read?
choices: Gap held, the read is on
Not filled till it holds a week

Short now with a tight stop

questions.lesson_line: Too stretched means wait. The bounce comes first.

wrong.Short now with a tight stop: A tight stop in a stretched stock just gets hit on the bounce.
wrong.Short now, momentum's down: Momentum is why it's stretched. 20% under the 9 EMA is double our 10% line.
wrong.Forget it, the move's over: It's not over, just stretched. Watch the bounce.

questions.simple: Skip it for now, because it's stretched far under the 9 EMA and stretched stocks bounce first.

deeper.counter: Stretch is measured from the 9 EMA, not from the high. A stock far off its high can sit near its 9 EMA after a long bounce, and that one isn't stretched.

questions.lesson_line: No new short within 3 sessions of a report. Check the date every time.

questions.lesson_line: Hard to borrow or a high fee, we pass.

questions.q: A big market flush just ended. That's a good time to press fresh shorts.
questions.why: False. Right after a big unwind is when shorts get hurt. Everyone who wanted out is already out, and the snapback can be violent. Don't ever be eager to short. Ever. Let the bounce happen first, then see if it fails. That's where a short read starts, not at the bottom of a flush.
questions.lesson_line: Never eager to short. Never right after a flush.
questions.simple: False, because right after a flush the selling is used up, and we're never eager to short.

questions.q: Two bounces run back into the gap zone. Which one sets up the better read for a short?
questions.why: The light one, with volume drying up. A quiet bounce tells you nobody's really buying. It's mostly sellers taking a break. Compare the bounce days to the gap day. If they trade less, the drift up has no real demand behind it. A loud bounce that closes up near the highs means buyers are winning, and I'd leave that one alone. Volume drying up raises the grade here. It isn't a must.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet bounce is weak. A loud one means buyers showed up.

wrong.Heavy volume, closing at highs: That's buyers winning the bounce. It undoes the read.
wrong.Volume rising every day: Buying is building. That's not a weak bounce.
wrong.Doesn't matter, only price: Price comes first, but volume drying up raises the grade.

questions.simple: The quiet bounce, because light volume shows little real buying as price drifts back up.

reasons: proposed card criterion (bg.light_bounce) awaiting the owner; Fleckenstein agrees

questions.q: What does this bounce tell you?
choices: Buyers are in control; stand down
The gap has to be a partial gap
questions.story: The bounce into the zone runs on more volume than the gap day and closes near its high.
questions.answer: Buyers are in control; stand down
questions.why: Buyers are in control. A strong, high-volume bounce that closes near its high is a pass or a lower grade.
questions.lesson_line: Strong bounce, strong close: stand down.

wrong.Sellers are in control; press: A strong close near the high is buyers in control.
wrong.Nothing; volume is noise: Volume on the bounce is one of the main tells.
wrong.The gap has to be a partial gap: Partial or full is the gap's size. It does not explain the bounce.

questions.q: How much do you trust this third gap?
choices: Not at all, it has no zone
questions.story: A stock gapped down off its top in March, then again in April. Now it gaps a third time and closes weak.
questions.why: Less. The first gap off the top is the one we read. In our study, later gaps off the same top did worse. By the third gap the stock's already been hit twice. You're late in the down cycle, and the easy part is gone. It still leaves a zone, but I'd treat it as a weaker read, not a stronger one.
questions.lesson_line: The first gap is the read. By the third, you're late.

wrong.More, the trend is clear: A clear downtrend means you're late. The easy part already happened.
wrong.Same, each gap stands alone: They don't. Later gaps off one top did worse.
wrong.Not at all, it has no zone: It still leaves a zone. It's just a weaker read.

questions.simple: Less, because later gaps off the same top did worse, and by the third you're late in the move.

deeper.trap: Each new gap feels like more proof the stock is broken. It works the other way. The first gap since the top is the read, and by the third the move is late.

questions.q: Short or not?
choices: Not a short; it is above the 200-day
Short; the gap is the signal
questions.story: A stock gapped down off a high. The bounce day closes 5.9% above its 200-day.
questions.answer: Not a short; it is above the 200-day
questions.why: Not a short. A gap in a stock still above its 200-day is a pullback in a leader. It closed 5.9% above the line.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day, a gap down is a pullback, not a short.

wrong.Short; the gap is the signal: The gap is a level, and the 200-day rule bars the short.
wrong.Short; the bounce day rejected: A rejection above the 200-day is still above the line.
wrong.Buy; gaps always fill: Gaps do not always fill. Only twenty-two percent closed the gap during the bounce in Bulkowski's sample.

questions.q: What's the problem with shorting this bounce?
choices: It's late, and big drops bounce
questions.story: This stock fell 35% on its gap day, on 27x volume. Twenty-four sessions later it bounces to the 20-day, already 40% off its high.
questions.answer: It's late, and big drops bounce
questions.why: It's late. This is BMRN. A 35% day leaves the 20-day sitting far under the gap zone. So this bounce to the 20-day never tests the level that matters. And the stock is already 40% off its high. You'd be shorting near the bottom of a move that already happened, and big drops bounce hard. I'd let this one go.
questions.lesson_line: After a huge drop, the 20-day sits far under the zone. That's late.

wrong.The volume was too heavy: Heavy volume is part of a textbook gap. That wasn't the flaw.
wrong.Twenty-four sessions is too long: DLTR's rejection also came 24 sessions after its gap. The wait wasn't it.
wrong.The 20-day is above the zone: Reverse. After a drop this big, the 20-day sits way under the zone.

questions.simple: It's a late short, because the stock already fell 40% and the bounce never gets near the gap zone.

deeper.trap: The stock looks weakest here, 40% off its high, so a short feels safe. The level that matters is far overhead. Compare DLTR: a 15% gap, then a flat five-week bounce to the 20-day under the 200-day.

questions.q: A big drop, then a dead-cat bounce that runs its course. What did Bulkowski find price does next?
questions.why: It falls again. In Bulkowski's dead-cat sample, the decline resumed after the bounce, about 30% from the bounce high in 49 days on average. But look at the order. The bounce came first, and that bounce alone averaged 28%. That's why we never short the gap day. You'd sit through the whole bounce. Let it finish, then read it.
questions.lesson_line: The bounce comes first. The next leg down comes after.

wrong.Fills the gap right away: The decline resumed after the bounce. No quick fill.
wrong.Rallies another 30% or so: The bounce was the rally. After it, price fell again, about 30% in 49 days on average.
wrong.Goes flat for a year: Price kept falling, about 30% in 49 days on average.

questions.simple: It falls again, so the time to look at a short is after the bounce, not before it.

deeper.trap: The 30% is an average over his sample, not a target for one stock. Use it for the order of things, bounce then decline, not for a price.

questions.q: In Bulkowski's dead-cat sample, what share closed the gap during the bounce?

questions.lesson_line: Most gaps stay open through the bounce.

wrong.58%: 58% is the share that closed it within 6 months, not during the bounce.
wrong.90%: Far too high. Even after 6 months, 58% had closed it.
wrong.38%: 38% is the share that had closed it by 3 months, not during the bounce.

questions.simple: Only 22% closed the gap during the bounce, so most gaps stayed open for a while.

questions.q: Kell calls a gap down from highs, followed by a Wedge Drop, a sign of a top.
questions.why: True. He says a gap down from highs, followed by a Wedge Drop, marked the 2021 top for DECK.
questions.lesson_line: A gap down from highs is a top warning.

questions.q: Four gap days off the same kind of top. Which one is the cleanest bear gap to mark?
choices: First gap, down 7%, closed near lows
Third gap, down 7%, closed near lows
First gap, down 3%, closed near highs
questions.answer: First gap, down 7%, closed near lows
questions.why: The first gap, down 7%, closed near the lows. It has all three things you want. It's the first gap off the top, it's a real hit, and the sellers won the close. The third gap closes just as weak, but it's late, and later gaps off one top did worse. Down 3% and closing near the highs is buyers fighting back. The second gap in the upper half has neither.
questions.lesson_line: First gap, big hit, weak close. That's the one.

wrong.Second gap, down 6%, upper half: It isn't the first gap, and buyers held the close up.
wrong.Third gap, down 7%, closed near lows: Same close, but it's the third gap. Later ones did worse.
wrong.First gap, down 3%, closed near highs: Buyers took a lot back. Small gap, strong close.

questions.simple: The first gap with a big drop and a weak close, because it's early and the sellers clearly won.

questions.q: What setup are you looking at?
choices: Gap Support, a gap on volume
questions.story: Four straight lower closes, two gap downs and rising volume. The fifth day gaps down again on the heaviest volume.
questions.why: Parabolic Long. Count what came before the gap. Four straight lower closes, two gaps down, volume building, then another gap on the heaviest volume. That's a burst down into a climax. A plain bear gap has none of that before it. It just gaps off a top. Same last bar, a totally different story.
questions.lesson_line: Count the days before the gap. A burst down is a different setup.

wrong.Bear gap off a top: A plain bear gap has no burst before it. This gap came after four lower closes and two gaps.
wrong.Parabolic Short, a climax gap: A Parabolic Short's climax day gaps up after a burst up. This one gapped down.
wrong.Gap Support, a gap on volume: Gap Support is a gap up whose zone is support. This stock gapped down.

questions.simple: It's a Parabolic Long, because the gap comes at the end of a run of lower closes and gaps down.

deeper.trap: Both shapes gap down on big volume, so the last bar can't tell them apart. Count what came before it. A run of lower closes and gaps down is a burst. A plain bear gap comes straight off a top.

questions.q: Worth marking as a bear gap?
choices: No, it's an ordinary down day
questions.story: The gap day. It opens 2.1% under the prior close, which is 0.89 ATR, less than its normal day's range. It never trades back to that close and finishes sharply lower.
questions.answer: No, it's an ordinary down day
questions.why: No, that's an ordinary down day. VZ opened 2.1% lower, which sounds like a gap. But ATR, the average true range, is how much a stock moves on a normal day. This open was 0.89 ATR, less than one normal day. A move that small doesn't trap many buyers, so there's no zone worth defending. Size a gap against the stock's own range, not the raw percent. The one you mark is a real shock to that stock.
questions.lesson_line: Size the gap against the stock's normal day. A small one is just a red day.

wrong.Yes, any gap down counts: A gap smaller than a normal day's range leaves nothing to defend.
wrong.Yes, it closed sharply lower: A red close doesn't make a gap day. The open was less than one ATR.
wrong.Yes, the gap never filled: Unfilled doesn't matter if the gap was tiny. 0.89 ATR is noise for VZ.

questions.simple: No, because the drop was smaller than a normal day for this stock, so not much is trapped above it.

deeper.trap: A 2.1% open can look like a gap. Size it against the stock's own range. Fleckenstein said the gap-down move should be a severe price decline relative to the stock's daily trading behavior.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Log it; the stop did its job
Widen the stop and short again
questions.story: A study short was taken on a clean rejection. A strong market stopped it the next day for a loss of 1R. The gap was textbook.
questions.answer: Log it; the stop did its job
questions.why: Log it. The stop is the exit and it only moves up. A textbook gap in a strong market is a planned loss of 1R.
questions.lesson_line: A planned loss is the cost of the trade. Take it and move on.

wrong.Widen the stop and short again: The stop is the exit. It never moves wider.
wrong.Short again at double size: Never add or double up. A new try needs a new setup, as a new trade.
wrong.Quit shorting for good: One planned loss is not a reason to quit. The market was the problem.

questions.q: Four of our study shorts lost, and every one had a textbook gap. What sank them?
choices: Just bad luck on the fills
questions.why: What surrounded the gap. In all four losers the gap itself was textbook. The gap is just the level. CIEN got stopped the next session in a strong market, with QQQ 1.0% over its 50-day. BMRN was shorted with the stock already 40% off its high. A perfect gap can't fix a bad bounce, the wrong market or a late entry.
questions.lesson_line: The gap is the level. The bounce, the market and how late you are decide the trade.

wrong.The gaps were too small: Every one was textbook. Size wasn't the problem.
wrong.Earnings came too soon: That's a separate check. It didn't decide these four.
wrong.Just bad luck on the fills: Fills weren't it. What surrounded the gap was.

questions.simple: What was around the gap sank them, because each gap was textbook and the bounce, market and timing were wrong.

deeper.example: CIEN and CHKP were both rejected at the 20-day after 19 to 23 sessions with tight stops, 1.3% and 2.4%. Both were stopped at once while the general market was in a strong uptrend.

questions.q: What is the read, and what is left open?

A buy; the gap will fill
Pass; the volume was too heavy
questions.story: A stock gaps down 15.2% on 15.1x volume, the first gap since its top. The zone is unfilled. A quiet five-week bounce reaches the 20-day, under the 200-day.
questions.answer: A clean level; the fall is not traded
questions.why: A clean level. Today the fall is measured, not traded, so we read the zone, the bounce and the market before any short.
questions.lesson_line: Read the level first. The short is a later decision.

wrong.A confirmed short; enter now: Today the app defines no trade. This is a read, not an entry.
wrong.A buy; the gap will fill: Only twenty-two percent closed the gap during the bounce in Bulkowski's sample.
wrong.Pass; the volume was too heavy: Heavy volume on the gap day is part of the read, not a flaw.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: A warning; let the stop decide
Add to the long near the low
Ignore it; it is above the 200-day
questions.story: You own a leader above its rising 200-day. It gaps down 9% off its high on earnings and closes in the lower half.
questions.answer: A warning; let the stop decide
questions.why: Treat it as a warning and let the stop decide. Our card says a bear gap off highs on your stock is a warning, managed by the trail and the gap rule. The stop is the exit and only moves up, never wider. Do not add, and do not short it: we short only below the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A gap down on your leader is a warning. The stop decides.

wrong.Add to the long near the low: Our rule is the full size at one price, with no adding.
wrong.Ignore it; it is above the 200-day: The 200-day bars a short here, but the warning stands. Keep your stop and trail.
wrong.Short it against your long: We short only below the 200-day. This leader is above it.

questions.simple: Treat it as a warning and let your stop and trail manage it, because the gap warns but does not decide.

deeper.trap: The gap rule is the one time the stop can move. Our rulebook says the stop is the exit and only moves up, never down or wider. The gap rule is the one exception. A gap through your stop is handled by that rule, not by hope. Never widen the stop to wait for a bounce.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, A5, B26)

questions.q: Shorting the gap-day close worked better in our test when SPY was under its 200-day.

The gap-day close is still a stretched stock with a stop way up over the high. A weak market helps the later retest, after the bounce fails. It can't rescue a bad entry.
questions.lesson_line: A weak market helps a good read. It won't rescue a reflex short.
questions.simple: False, because that short did worse with SPY under its 200-day, so a weak market alone is no edge.

deeper.trap: It sounds logical that a weak market makes any short better. Our test found the opposite for the gap-day close. A weak market helps the later retest, not a short with a wide stop into a stretched stock.

questions.q: What's your read?

A confirmed short at the open
A buy, the window fills soon
questions.story: A stock topped, then 23 sessions later opened 7.9% lower. It closed down 13.5% on 6.7x volume and left a full window, its first gap since the top. Fifteen sessions later the bounce stalled under the falling 20-day and the zone.
questions.answer: A first gap, a zone to watch
questions.why: A first gap and a zone to watch. Walk it through. Full window, a 13.5% hit on 6.7x volume, the first gap off the top. Then a bounce that stalls under the falling 20-day and under the zone. Sellers are sitting right where you'd expect. That's OI in 2011, and it's still not a trade by itself. A short would also need the stock under its 200-day and a Red or Orange market, and you don't know either here.
questions.lesson_line: A full window and a bounce that stalls under it. Watch it, don't jump it.

wrong.A buy, the window fills soon: The bounce stalled under the zone. Don't count on a fill.
wrong.Nothing, the stall ends it: The stall is the read. Only a close over the top edge ends it.

questions.simple: A zone to watch, because it's a clean first gap and the bounce stalled under it.

deeper.trap: The stalled bounce makes it look like a done deal. It isn't. The read tells you where sellers wait, not that a trade exists.

We don't trade off it.

wrong.No, it's above its 200-day: The bounce ran under the 200-day. That box is checked.
wrong.Yes, it closed over its 20-day: It closed back under the 20-day. A rejection closes back under the level.

questions.q: The bounce on this chart tagged its falling 20-day on the last bar. Is that a rejection you can read?

No, it has to reach the zone

A rejection needs the close to roll back under the level, down near the low. A bar that tags it and finishes strong is half the story. Wait for the day that closes weak.

wrong.Yes, it tagged the 20-day: Tagging it is half. The close has to roll over too.
wrong.Yes, the gap is still open: An open gap isn't enough. The bounce has to fail.
wrong.No, it has to reach the zone: Right call, wrong reason. The falling 20-day counts as a level.

questions.why: True. All 10 scan examples were full windows, the stricter form: the gap day's high stayed under the prior day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Our clean examples were full windows, not partial gaps.

questions.q: Fleckenstein, Bulkowski and our lesson all agree on what?
choices: Wait for the bounce before any short
questions.answer: Wait for the bounce before any short
questions.why: Wait for the bounce. Fleckenstein waits for it to exhaust itself, Bulkowski shorts the top of it, and we never short the close by reflex.
questions.lesson_line: The bounce comes before any short.

wrong.Short the gap-day close: That is the reflex short we warn against.
wrong.Buy the gap-day low: None of the three says to buy the low of a gap day.
wrong.Hold until the gap fills: A fill ends the read. None of them waits for it.

questions.q: Shorting the gap-day close and shorting the failed bounce are the same trade.
questions.why: False. The gap-day close runs into a bounce that averaged 28% for big drops. The failed bounce is a later, different entry.
questions.lesson_line: Same gap, different trade. The close and the bounce are not the same.

questions.q: Which stock had the bear gap day?
choices: Stock A; Stock B is a News Failure
Stock B; it bounced the hardest
Neither; the news was priced in
questions.story: Two stocks open down 6% on bad news. Stock A closes down 5.8%, in the lower third of its range. Stock B closes 0.5% above the prior close.
questions.answer: Stock A; Stock B is a News Failure
questions.why: Stock A. It closed down more than 5% in the lower third. Stock B closed above the prior close, so the news failed.
questions.lesson_line: Same open, different close. The close names the setup.

wrong.Stock B; it bounced the hardest: A close above the prior close means the news failed. That is a buy, not a bear gap.

questions.simple: Both stop you, because it's above its 200-day and its report is only 2 sessions away.

deeper.trap: The chart checks every box we read: a first gap, a weak close, a rejection at the 20-day. That's what makes it tempting to wave the rules through. One failed rule is enough to skip it.

questions.why: True. Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally.

questions.q: Even on a perfect chart, you never hold more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.
questions.why: True. 1% of the average daily volume is our cap, clean chart or not. The point is getting out. Own a big chunk of what trades in a day, and your own selling moves the price against you. That hurts most when everyone's heading for the door at once, like on a bear gap. Check the average volume before you size, and treat 1% as a ceiling, not a target.
questions.lesson_line: 1% of average daily volume is the most we hold. A ceiling, not a target.
questions.simple: True, because owning more than that makes it hard to get out without moving the price yourself.

questions.lesson_line: Take 1% of the average daily volume. That's the most you hold.

questions.q: Which one is the better spot to read a short?
choices: Neither, we don't short under it
BKLR, it has further to fall
questions.story: Two stocks print the same bear gap, and both close under their 200-day. ZNTR's 200-day is falling. BKLR's is still rising.
questions.why: ZNTR, but only by a little. Both pass the line that matters, a close under the 200-day. The slope is a tiebreaker. A falling 200-day means the long-term trend has already turned down. A rising one means the bigger trend is still up. Don't overrate it though. In our study 27% of shorts under a falling 200-day reached 3R, against 25% under a rising one. A small edge.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day is the line. A falling one is a small plus, nothing more.

wrong.BKLR, the rising 200-day: A rising 200-day means the bigger trend is still up. That's the weaker of the two.
wrong.Neither, we don't short under it: Backwards. Under the 200-day is the only place we short.
wrong.BKLR, it has further to fall: Room to fall isn't the read. The trend behind the stock is.

questions.simple: ZNTR, because its falling 200-day means the long-term trend already turned down, though the edge is small.

questions.q: What does that close do to your read?
questions.story: A stock gapped down off its highs, bounced, and got turned back at its falling 50-day. Today it closes back above that 50-day.
questions.why: It switches the read off. The whole read was that sellers held the 50-day. A close back above it says they didn't hold it this time. Buyers took the line back. A higher price can look like a better short, and that's exactly the trap. The evidence you were leaning on is gone. Move on.
questions.lesson_line: Close back over the line the bounce failed at, and the read is done.

wrong.Confirms the read: A close back over the line the bounce failed at ends the read. It confirms nothing.
wrong.Gives a better short price: A close back over the line is buyers winning. The read ends, it doesn't improve.
wrong.Nothing, only the 200-day counts: The 50-day the bounce failed at was the whole read. A close over it ends it.

questions.simple: It ends the read, because the stock closed back above the 50-day line where the bounce had failed.

deeper.trap: A close back over the 50-day can look like a better price to short, since the stock is higher. The line the bounce failed at was the evidence for the read. Once price closes back over it, the evidence is gone.

reasons: one source: the criteria card (no outside source for the 50-day line)

questions.q: A stock closes back above its 200-day during the retest. The short read is over.
questions.why: True. Under the 200-day is where shorts live for us. Once it closes back above, it's out of short territory. That close also tells you buyers are stronger than the gap made it look. Take it off your short list.
questions.lesson_line: Close back over the 200-day and the short read is over.
questions.simple: True, because we only short below the 200-day, so a close back above it ends the read.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: A bounce on heavy volume that closes near its high is a reason to stand down.
questions.why: True. That bounce shows buyers in control. It is the opposite of the weak, light bounce Fleckenstein wants.
questions.lesson_line: A strong bounce that closes near its high means stand down.

questions.q: What do you do with the read?
choices: Keep it, the stock is still weak
questions.story: A bear gap sits under its 200-day in a weak group. This week our app's market reading flips to Green, and breadth thrusts higher.
questions.why: Stand down. A short needs the market falling with it, a Red or Orange reading. Green with breadth thrusting is the opposite, a market lifting most stocks. Two clean shorts in our study got stopped right away in a strong market. The stock can stay on your radar. Just don't press it here.
questions.lesson_line: Market flips Green with breadth thrusting. Stand down on the short read.

wrong.Keep it, the stock is still weak: The chart is only part of it. The short needs the market's help.
wrong.Short it at half size: Half size doesn't bring the market's help back.
wrong.Ignore it, only the 200-day counts: The 200-day is one check. A Green market says stand down anyway.

questions.simple: Stand down, because a short needs a weak market, and a Green market with strong breadth takes that help away.

deeper.trap: The stock's own chart still looks weak, so keeping the read feels right. The market's help is part of the short. When that help goes, stand down.

questions.q: A climax day ranges 40.00 to 48.00 and closes at 45.00. Where in its range did it close, in percent?

questions.lesson_line: Close minus low, over high minus low. Middle or higher fits the climax day.
questions.simple: It closed 62.5% up its range, above the middle, which fits a climax day that closes mid or high.

questions.q: Once you're in, you don't move the stop further away to give the trade room.
questions.why: True. The stop is the exit, and it only moves one way, in your favor. Up on a long, down on a short. Widening it to give room is how a small loss turns into a big one. The one exception is our gap rule. When a gap jumps your stop, the first 30 minutes set the new one. That's a rule for a gap, not room for a trade that isn't working.
questions.lesson_line: Never widen the stop to give a trade room.
questions.simple: True, because the stop is the exit and we never widen it, except under the gap rule.

deeper.trap: On a short, wider means higher. The stop is never moved higher after entry. On a gap up over the stop, the first 30-minute high is the new stop. You're out if the loss passes 2R.

reasons: rests on one rulebook line (h02)

questions.story: You own a leader. It gaps down overnight and opens under your stop. Part of you wants to wait for a bounce.
questions.q: What sets your new stop?
choices: The low of the first 30-minute bar
The low of the day, at the close
The prior day's low, above the gap
The low of the first 5-minute bar
questions.answer: The low of the first 30-minute bar
questions.why: The low of the first 30-minute bar. That's our gap rule. The gap already blew through your stop, so the first 30 minutes of the day decide. That low is your new stop. If those 30 minutes push the loss past 2R, you're out. No hoping for a bounce. It's the one time the stop moves down, and it has a hard ceiling on it.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through your stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

wrong.The low of the day, at the close: We don't wait for the close. The first 30 minutes of the gap day decide.
wrong.The prior day's low, above the gap: That's above where it's trading. The gap day's first 30-minute low is the new stop.
wrong.The low of the first 5-minute bar: Too short. The rule uses the first 30-minute bar.

questions.simple: The low of the first 30-minute bar, because the gap rule lets the first 30 minutes decide.

deeper.trap: Waiting for a bounce feels patient, and that's the trap. The first 30 minutes set the new stop, and past 2R you get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20, A4)

questions.q: The retest read waits for a bounce to fail. Where do you watch for that failure?
choices: Back up at the old high
The 9 EMA in the first week

A bounce that tags one and closes weak back under it, that's the failure you're waiting for. It can't close above the zone's top edge on the way, or the gap's filled and the read is off. The 200-day decides whether you can short at all. And shorting is only for traders who've already made $1 million trading.
questions.lesson_line: The retest read is a bounce into the zone or a falling 20 or 50-day that fails.

wrong.The 200-day, tested from below: The 200-day decides if you can short. The bounce fails lower, at the zone or a falling 20 or 50-day.
wrong.Back up at the old high: By then the gap is long filled and the read is gone.
wrong.The 9 EMA in the first week: The 9 EMA is where a stretched stock snaps back to. The bounce fails higher, at the zone or the 20 or 50-day.

questions.simple: Watch the zone or a falling 20-day or 50-day, because that's where sellers step back in.
